activities.description: Validate home blood pressure monitoring technique. Ensure readings are taken after 5 minutes of quiet rest, with back and arm supported, legs uncrossed, and cuff at heart level. Advise against taking readings immediately after exercise (e.g., cycling) or within 30 minutes of caffeine/tobacco use.
activities.timing: At next visit or via telehealth education

activities.description: Review home blood pressure log to assess control trends. Target for general adult population is SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg, unless comorbidities dictate otherwise.
Assess renal function (serum creatinine/eGFR) and electrolytes to evaluate for potential end-organ effects of hypertension and guide safe medication management.
Consider lipid profile and fasting glucose/HbA1c to assess overall cardiovascular risk, given established hypertension.

Review adherence to amlodipine 5 mg daily. Discuss barriers related to rotating work shifts and strategies to improve consistency (e.g., pill organizers, alarm reminders). Confirm patient understanding of the importance of regular intake for blood pressure control.

Counsel on lifestyle modifications: limit salt intake to <5g/day, maintain healthy weight (BMI <23 kg/m²), engage in regular physical activity (30 minutes daily), and avoid tobacco and excessive alcohol use.
Schedule follow-up with general practitioner to review blood pressure control, adherence strategies, and investigation results.
Clarify allergy status. Current record states 'allergy status not documented' with unconfirmed verification status. Confirm any known drug or non-drug allergies to ensure safe prescribing practices.

Confirm current medication status. While amlodipine 5 mg daily is recorded in history, the resource status is 'unknown'. Verify if the patient is currently taking this medication and if any other antihypertensives or supplements are being used.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

Review current antihypertensive regimen (losartan 50 mg daily) for adherence, timing, and potential contribution to lightheadedness or orthostatic symptoms. Verify if the medication is currently being taken as prescribed.

Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. activities.description: Confirm the exact dose and frequency of amlodipine currently being taken, and verify adherence patterns over the past 18 months.
Document specific drug allergies, including severity and reaction type, as current status is unconfirmed.
Order renal function panel (serum creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes) to assess for hypertensive nephropathy and baseline kidney function.
Order fasting lipid profile to evaluate cardiovascular risk factors associated with hypertension.
Perform standardized clinic blood pressure measurement using correct cuff size, seated position, and rest period, per hypertension guidelines.
Counsel on lifestyle modifications including sodium restriction (<5g/day), regular physical activity (30 mins daily), and weight management.
Advise on home blood pressure monitoring technique and consider provision of a validated home monitor for ongoing tracking.
Conduct comprehensive medication reconciliation to verify amlodipine use, check for potential interactions, and assess need for dose adjustment by prescribing clinician.
Schedule in-person primary care visit within 1 month to review investigation results, confirm medication regimen, and reassess blood pressure control.

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor blood pressure closely. Given the patient's age (68 years), assess orthostatic blood pressure at every visit to evaluate for postural hypotension, which is a risk factor for falls and may influence management decisions.
Obtain recent serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to assess renal function and screen for hypertensive nephropathy or chronic kidney disease.
activities.timing: During urgent same-day review or within 1 week

activities.description: Perform urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) to screen for albuminuria, a marker of end-organ damage and cardiovascular risk.
activities.timing: During urgent same-day review or within 1 week

activities.description: Conduct a comprehensive metabolic panel including electrolytes (particularly potassium and sodium) to assess for electrolyte disturbances that may influence antihypertensive therapy safety.
activities.timing: During urgent same-day review or within 1 week

activities.description: Perform a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) to screen for left ventricular hypertrophy, ischemic changes, or arrhythmias associated with long-standing hypertension.
activities.timing: During urgent same-day review or within 1 week

activities.description: Review current adherence to amlodipine 10 mg daily. Verify if the patient has been taking the medication regularly and correctly, as non-adherence is a common cause of uncontrolled hypertension.

Conduct a generic medication review to identify potential drug-drug interactions, over-the-counter medication use (e.g., NSAIDs, decongestants), and supplements that may elevate blood pressure or interact with amlodipine.

Advise on dietary modifications: limit salt intake to less than 5g per day, increase consumption of fruits and vegetables, and prefer healthy oils and omega-3 rich foods such as fish, nuts, and seeds.
Recommend regular physical activity: aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise daily, as tolerated and approved by the treating clinician after urgent stabilization.
Advise against tobacco and alcohol use, as both are significant risk factors for hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
Encourage weight management: aim for a BMI less than 23 kg/m² and waist circumference less than 80 cm for women, if applicable to the patient's current body habitus.
Schedule a follow-up appointment within 1-2 weeks after the urgent review to reassess blood pressure control, review investigation results, and adjust management plan if necessary.

Clarify allergy status: The record states 'allergy status not documented'. Confirm if the patient has any known drug allergies, particularly to calcium channel blockers or other antihypertensive classes.
Clarify current medication status: The MedicationStatement for amlodipine has status 'unknown'. Confirm if the patient is currently taking amlodipine 10 mg daily, has stopped it, or is unsure.

activities.description: Monitor glycemic control with HbA1c testing every 3 months given current value of 8.1% (above typical target of <7.0%) and persistent hyperglycemia.
Encourage self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) including fasting and post-prandial values to assess impact of irregular meal times and night-shift work patterns.
Obtain urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) to screen for diabetic nephropathy, as this is currently unrecorded.
Perform dilated retinal examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy, as the last screening date is unknown.
Assess renal function (serum creatinine/eGFR) and electrolytes (potassium) as part of routine diabetes monitoring.
Obtain fasting lipid profile to assess cardiovascular risk, given the association between diabetes and dyslipidemia.
Measure blood pressure and assess for hypertension, a common comorbidity in type 2 diabetes.
Provide dietary counseling focusing on reducing consumption of sugary beverages (e.g., sugary tea) and establishing regular meal times compatible with night-shift work to improve glycemic control.
Discuss strategies for managing irregular eating patterns associated with night-shift work, such as preparing balanced snacks and avoiding large meals before sleep.

Review current metformin therapy (500 mg twice daily) for adherence, tolerability, and efficacy. Verify if the patient is currently taking the medication as prescribed, noting the resource status is 'unknown'.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently documented as 'not documented' and 'unconfirmed'.
Confirm current medication use of metformin 500 mg twice daily, as the FHIR resource status is 'unknown' despite a recorded history.
Schedule follow-up appointment to review glycemic control, lifestyle modifications, and results of pending preventive screenings (retinal exam, urine ACR).

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Review and adjust sulfonylurea (gliclazide) dosage to mitigate hypoglycemia risk. Evaluate renal function and HbA1c to guide long-term diabetes management. Counsel on consistent meal timing relative to medication administration. Preserve the supplied clinician disposition: urgent. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Conduct urgent same-day review of gliclazide 80 mg regimen in the context of recent hypoglycemia (62 mg/dL) associated with skipped meals. Evaluate the appropriateness of current sulfonylurea dosing for a 72-year-old patient, considering renal function and hypoglycemia risk.
Obtain renal function tests (serum creatinine, eGFR) to assess drug clearance capacity and guide medication safety, as renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk with sulfonylureas.
Measure HbA1c to evaluate long-term glycemic control and inform whether current treatment intensity is appropriate for the patient's age and comorbidities.
Implement structured self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG), including pre-prandial and post-prandial checks, to identify patterns of hypoglycemia and assess response to any medication adjustments.

Counsel on the importance of consistent meal timing relative to gliclazide administration. Emphasize that skipping meals while on sulfonylureas significantly increases hypoglycemia risk. Discuss strategies for managing missed meals.
Educate patient and spouse on recognizing early symptoms of hypoglycemia (sweating, confusion, weakness) and appropriate immediate management (fast-acting carbohydrates).
Verify allergy status, as current record indicates 'allergy status not documented'. Confirm any known drug or food allergies to ensure safe medication management.
Clarify the value and timing of the second reported low blood glucose episode to fully characterize the frequency and severity of recent hypoglycemic events.
Schedule follow-up within 1-2 weeks to review renal function, HbA1c results, and SMBG logs. Re-evaluate medication regimen based on these findings and patient's adherence to meal timing.

Consider referral to endocrinology or diabetes specialist if hypoglycemia persists despite medication adjustment and lifestyle counseling, or if renal function significantly impacts treatment options.

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

activities.description: Assess asthma control over the preceding 4 weeks, specifically evaluating frequency of daytime symptoms, night-time awakenings, activity limitation, and reliever inhaler use. Current reports of weekly cough and 4 days/week reliever use suggest inadequate control.

Observe and assess inhaler technique for both the budesonide/formoterol maintenance inhaler and the salbutamol reliever inhaler. Correct technique if errors are identified, particularly given the recent supply of a new device.

Consider spirometry (FEV1/FVC) or Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) measurement to objectively assess airflow limitation and reversibility, aiding in confirmation of control status and diagnosis if not recently performed.

Review adherence to the prescribed budesonide/formoterol maintenance regimen. Discuss barriers to adherence and verify the specific strength and dosing schedule currently being used, as these are currently unknown in the record.

Evaluate the need for step-up therapy in asthma management given the current pattern of symptoms (weekly night-time cough and frequent reliever use), which indicates inadequate control. This review should be conducted by the treating clinician.

Develop or update a written asthma action plan. Include instructions on daily management, recognition of worsening symptoms, and specific steps to take during an exacerbation, including when to seek urgent care.
Provide patient education on asthma triggers, the importance of adherence to maintenance therapy, and proper inhaler technique. Discuss strategies to minimize exposure to identified triggers.

Document and verify allergy status. Current record indicates allergy status is not documented; clarify any known drug or environmental allergies that may impact asthma management or medication selection.
Schedule a follow-up review in 4-12 weeks to reassess asthma control, adherence, and inhaler technique. Adjust management plan based on response to current therapy and any changes made.
Consider referral to a respiratory specialist if asthma remains poorly controlled despite optimized therapy, or if there is diagnostic uncertainty regarding the cause of persistent cough.

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring

* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Initiate a symptom diary to correlate respiratory symptoms (wheezing, breathlessness) with work exposure (flour handling) versus time away from work. Record frequency, severity, and use of rescue medication.
Monitor asthma control using standard criteria (daytime symptoms, night-time awakenings, activity limitation, and rescue inhaler use) over the preceding four weeks.
Consider spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility testing to objectively assess airflow obstruction and support evaluation for occupational asthma.
Refer to occupational health services or a pulmonologist for specialized assessment of potential occupational asthma triggers, given the temporal relationship between flour exposure and symptoms.
Review current use of budesonide/formoterol inhaler. Verify prescription details, dosage, and frequency, as these are currently unknown. Assess inhaler technique and adherence.
Discuss workplace exposure reduction strategies, such as engineering controls or personal protective equipment, in consultation with occupational health.
Schedule a routine follow-up appointment to review symptom diary, spirometry results (if performed), and medication adherence. Reassess asthma control and adjust management plan as needed.

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Assess asthma control frequency (symptoms >2 days/week reported) and review for nocturnal symptoms or activity limitation. Monitor for signs of exacerbation such as increased rescue inhaler use or reduced peak expiratory flow.
Observe patient's inhaler technique directly to identify mechanical barriers related to hand osteoarthritis. Assess hand function and grip strength if not recently evaluated.

Consider referral to respiratory physiotherapy or occupational therapy for assessment of alternative inhaler devices (e.g., soft mist, dry powder with lower actuation force, or spacer-assisted MDI) suitable for limited hand dexterity.
Engage the patient's daughter in device training sessions to assist with inhaler actuation and adherence support. Discuss environmental trigger avoidance strategies.

Review current beclometasone and salbutamol prescriptions for appropriateness given reported missed doses. Verify if current devices are compatible with patient's hand function. Do not change regimen without clinician assessment.
Schedule follow-up in 4-12 weeks to reassess asthma control, inhaler technique, and adherence after any device adjustments or education interventions.
Clarify documented allergy status, as current record indicates 'allergy status not documented'.
Clarify specific prescription schedules and strengths for beclometasone and salbutamol, as these are currently unknown.
Clarify observed device use history to determine if previous technique assessments were performed.

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### SYMPTOMS
* **Classic symptoms**
    * Recurrent/ episodic wheezing
    * Breathlessness
    * Cough and/ or chest tightness
* **Supportive features**
    * History of atopy, family history of asthma, presence of triggers, presence of rhonchi on chest auscultation
    * No alternative explanation for these symptoms

activities.description: Obtain the specific discharge medication list, including product names, doses, and frequencies, as the current record only notes 'discharge inhaler regimen; products and doses unavailable'.
Verify the patient's allergy status, which is currently documented as 'not documented' and 'unconfirmed'.
Identify the recent trigger for the asthma exacerbation, as this information is currently missing.
Conduct a generic clinician medication review to verify the patient has access to the prescribed discharge inhalers and to assess adherence and inhaler technique.
Assess asthma control over the preceding four weeks, including daytime symptoms, night-time awakenings, activity limitation, and rescue inhaler use frequency.
Consider spirometry or peak expiratory flow (PEF) measurement to objectively assess lung function and establish a baseline for future monitoring.
Provide patient education on asthma triggers, warning signs of exacerbation, and proper inhaler technique.
Reconstruct and provide a written asthma action plan to the patient.
Schedule a follow-up review in 4-12 weeks to reassess disease control and modulate treatment if necessary.

* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

activities.description: Verify allergy status. Current record indicates 'allergy status not documented' with unconfirmed verification status. Confirm presence or absence of drug or environmental allergies to inform safe medication selection.

Review trigger avoidance strategies. Identify and minimize exposure to known asthma triggers (e.g., allergens, irritants, occupational exposures).
Schedule follow-up in 4-12 weeks to reassess asthma control, medication adherence, and inhaler technique. Adjust management plan based on response.

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

review_notes: Patient reports symptoms three days per week, which may indicate inadequate asthma control per standard criteria (symptoms >2 times/week).
Interrupted supply of maintenance inhaler due to cost is a critical barrier to adherence and control; addressing affordability is a priority.
Smoking status (8 cigarettes/day) is a significant risk factor for poor asthma control and exacerbations; cessation support is recommended.
Allergy status is unconfirmed; verification is necessary for safe medication management.
No specific medication changes are recommended; clinician should review current regimen and adjust based on control assessment and access issues.

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and ability to speak in full sentences during the urgent assessment. Watch for signs of severe exacerbation such as increased work of breathing, agitation, or desaturation.
Assess peak expiratory flow (PEF) if available, comparing to personal best if known, to help determine severity of exacerbation.
Review current budesonide/formoterol inhaler regimen details, including dose and frequency, as these are currently unavailable. Assess inhaler technique and adherence.
Clarify allergy status, which is currently undocumented, to ensure safe medication management.
Determine if the patient has a written asthma action plan and if they know their personal-best peak flow.
Educate on trigger avoidance and the importance of adherence to maintenance therapy. Discuss signs of worsening asthma requiring urgent care.
Schedule follow-up outpatient visit within one week after stabilization to assess response to treatment and adjust management if needed.
Consider referral to a pulmonologist or asthma specialist if asthma remains poorly controlled despite optimized therapy, or if there is diagnostic uncertainty.
activities.timing: Conditional on response to initial management

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

activities.description: Monitor for signs of COPD exacerbation, including increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, or increased sputum purulence. Assess symptom stability using the mMRC dyspnea scale.
Monitor room-air oxygen saturation to ensure adequate oxygenation, particularly if symptoms worsen.
Assess inhaler technique and adherence to current tiotropium therapy to ensure optimal drug delivery.
Review vaccination status for influenza and pneumococcal disease to ensure appropriate prophylaxis.
Refer to smoking cessation services or discuss pharmacological and behavioral support for tobacco cessation, given the patient's desire to stop smoking.
Counsel on smoking cessation as a primary intervention to slow disease progression and reduce exacerbation risk.

Perform a generic review of current respiratory medications, including tiotropium, to assess efficacy, side effects, and adherence. Do not initiate, stop, or change doses without clinician evaluation.
Schedule routine follow-up in 3 to 6 months for mild to moderate COPD, or sooner if symptoms worsen or exacerbations occur.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently undocumented.
Clarify the annual exacerbation count to assist in severity classification and management planning.

evidence_sources.original_text:
Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

Current breathlessness limits activities of daily living (shopping) but has been stable for 6 months.
Room-air oxygen saturation is 94% (recorded 2026-10-24), which is within acceptable limits for stable COPD.

Allergy status is explicitly documented as 'not documented' and 'unconfirmed'. This must be clarified before initiating any new therapies.
Patient requests assistance with local pulmonary rehabilitation due to transportation barriers. This is a key social determinant of health affecting adherence and outcomes.
No acute red flags (e.g., hemoptysis, weight loss, fever) are reported in the narrative, supporting a routine disposition.

ICMR context (S1) suggests spirometry is essential for severity assessment and follow-up intervals depend on severity (3-6 months for mild/moderate). Since severity is not fully quantified in the record, routine follow-up is recommended pending spirometry review.

activities.description: Obtain the previous hospital discharge summary to reconcile medications, confirm the specific inhaler devices prescribed, and verify the status of any pulmonary rehabilitation referrals.
Document allergy status, as it is currently recorded as unconfirmed/not documented.

Perform a generic medication review to identify the two discharge inhalers by name and device type. Verify the patient's understanding of the specific regimen (dose, frequency, and timing) for each inhaler.
Assess inhaler technique for both devices to ensure correct usage and optimal drug delivery.
Monitor room-air oxygen saturation and assess for signs of hypoxemia or hypercapnia, noting the previous reading of 95% on 2026-10-24.
Consider spirometry to document airflow obstruction and assess disease severity if not recently performed, to guide long-term management.
Counsel on smoking cessation if applicable, and discuss avoidance of other respiratory risk factors such as occupational exposures or solid fuel use.
Verify if a referral to pulmonary rehabilitation has been made or completed; if not, consider referral to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life.
Schedule a routine follow-up appointment with the primary care provider or pulmonologist to review inhaler regimen, technique, and symptom control.

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Monitor weight trends and appetite status at each visit to assess progression of unintentional weight loss.
Monitor respiratory symptoms and oxygen saturation to ensure COPD remains at baseline and to detect exacerbations.
Investigate causes of unintentional weight loss and poor appetite, including screening for nutritional deficiencies, malignancy, or other systemic causes.
Assess spirometry and COPD severity if not recently performed, to guide ongoing management.
Refer to primary care or appropriate specialist for comprehensive evaluation of weight loss and appetite changes.
Consider referral to social services or dietary support given the patient lives alone and reports fatigue with cooking.
Discuss strategies to manage fatigue during meal preparation, such as batch cooking or simplified meal options, to support adequate nutritional intake.
Review current COPD medication regimen, including tiotropium inhaler technique and adherence, to ensure optimal symptom control.
Review all current medications for potential side effects contributing to poor appetite or weight loss.
Schedule routine follow-up to reassess weight, appetite, and COPD symptoms.
Clarify patient's height to calculate BMI and assess nutritional status more accurately.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently undocumented.
Clarify history of weight-loss investigations to avoid duplication and guide further testing.
Clarify dietary assessment results or current nutritional intake patterns.

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Verify the specific name, strength, and device type of the current maintenance inhaler to ensure appropriate therapy for spirometry-established COPD.
Confirm documented allergy status, as current records indicate 'allergy status not documented'.
Obtain history of COPD exacerbations in the past 12 months to assist in severity classification and risk stratification.
Review vaccination records, specifically for influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, which are recommended for patients with COPD.
Clinician to review the verified inhaler regimen for appropriateness based on confirmed severity and symptom burden. Assess inhaler technique and adherence at the next visit.
Monitor respiratory symptoms, including dyspnea (using mMRC scale if applicable), cough, and sputum characteristics. Track room-air oxygen saturation periodically.
Counsel on low-cost ventilation improvements (e.g., opening windows, using exhaust fans if available) and safe fuel handling practices to reduce indoor air pollution exposure from solid-fuel cooking.
Provide education on recognizing signs of COPD exacerbation (increased dyspnea, sputum volume/purulence) and when to seek urgent care.
Schedule routine primary care follow-up in 3 to 6 months for stable mild-to-moderate COPD, or sooner if symptoms worsen or exacerbations occur.
Refer to a pulmonologist or higher center if symptoms remain uncontrolled despite optimized therapy, if complications develop, or if there is suspicion of alternative diagnoses.

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.
Monitor oxygen saturation continuously or at frequent intervals during urgent assessment to detect further desaturation or response to initial management.
Monitor respiratory rate, heart rate, and blood pressure to assess for signs of severe exacerbation or hemodynamic instability.
Obtain arterial blood gas analysis if oxygen saturation remains low or if there is concern for hypercapnia/respiratory failure.
activities.timing: As clinically indicated during urgent assessment

activities.description: Perform chest radiography to rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other acute pathology contributing to exacerbation.
Assess sputum characteristics (color, volume, purulence) and consider sputum culture if bacterial infection is suspected.
Check temperature to evaluate for fever, which may indicate infectious etiology.
Review current use of tiotropium inhaler, including technique and adherence. Verify if other rescue inhalers (e.g., short-acting beta-agonists) are available and being used appropriately.

Conduct a complete medication reconciliation to identify all current medications, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, to assess for potential interactions or contributors to exacerbation.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently undocumented. This is critical before initiating any new pharmacological interventions.
Clarify sputum color and presence of hemoptysis to help differentiate between infectious and non-infectious causes of exacerbation.
Clarify current temperature to assess for fever.
Advise on smoking cessation if applicable, as this is a key risk factor for COPD progression and exacerbations.
activities.timing: Conditional on completion of urgent evaluation

activities.description: Arrange follow-up within one week after discharge or stabilization to review response to treatment, inhaler technique, and adjust long-term management plan.
Consider referral to pulmonology if exacerbation is severe, unresponsive to initial management, or if there are complications such as respiratory failure.

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake

        * Symptomatic -> **No** -> Clinical Follow-up

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly
